# Volume 2 — XXIX Poetry and Prose

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

During the following month, Nell resided in a state that, by Brierley's standards, could be considered a whirlwind of activity. Preparing her own simple wardrobe for Wexcombe took a back seat. Miss Rosalind was preparing for her wedding, making the stone residence the hub of perpetual deliberations, arrangements, and debates, while Belinda the Fourth lingered nearby in flustered joy and amazement. Afterwards, the seamstress arrived, bringing the delight and misery associated with selecting styles and undergoing fittings. Nell and Isolde passed half of their time at Echo Cottage, and on certain nights, Nell lay awake worrying if she had given proper counsel when she suggested that Miss Rosalind pick brown instead of navy blue for her going-away attire, and choose a princess style for her gray silk.
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0000 }

All who were involved in the tale of Miss Rosalind experienced great happiness. As soon as he learned the news from his father, Cedric Stanhope hurried over to Grey Shutters so that he and Nell could discuss it together.
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0001 }

“I was sure father could be relied upon to choose a lovely little second mother for me,” he stated with pride. “Teacher, it is wonderful to possess a father you can rely on. Miss Rosalind has earned my absolute love. Grandma feels happy as well. She remarks that she is truly relieved father refrained from choosing an American as his second spouse, since, even if matters worked out well on the initial occasion, a similar outcome would probably not occur a second time. Mrs. Sowerby mentions that the union has her complete approval, and she considers it probable that Miss Rosalind will abandon her odd ideas and resemble ordinary folks, now that her marriage is approaching. However, teacher, my wish is that she keeps her odd ideas, since I enjoy them. Furthermore, I do not desire her to resemble ordinary folks. As things stand, there are far too many ordinary folks about. Teacher, you understand.”
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0002 }

Belinda the Fourth represented an additional person who was radiant.
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0003 }

“Oh, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, everything has ended up so wonderful. As soon as Mr. Stanhope and Miss Rosalind return from their tower, I am permitted to travel to Boston and reside alongside them . . . even though I am merely fifteen, whereas the remaining girls did not leave until reaching sixteen. Isn't Mr. Stanhope magnificent? He simply adores the very earth she walks upon, and observing the expression in his eyes while he looks at her gives me such a strange feeling at times. It is beyond words, Miss Harcourt, ma’am. I am terribly grateful that they care for one another so deeply. When everything is considered, it is the finest manner to be, even if certain people are able to manage without it. I have an aunt who was wedded three separate times and claims that her first marriage was for love while the final two were purely for business, and she experienced happiness with every one of them except during the funerals. However, I believe she ran a resk, Miss Harcourt, ma’am.”
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0004 }

“Oh, it’s all so romantic,” Nell whispered to Thirza later that evening. “If I hadn’t chosen the incorrect route the day we traveled to Mr. Kimball’s, I would never have become acquainted with Miss Rosalind; and if I hadn’t encountered her, I would never have brought Cedric there . . . and he would never have sent a letter to his father regarding a visit to Miss Rosalind at the exact moment Mr. Stanhope was departing for San Francisco. Mr. Stanhope mentions that as soon as he received that correspondence, he decided to dispatch his associate to San Francisco and travel to this place rather than going himself. He had not received any news concerning Miss Rosalind in fifteen years. At that time, someone had informed him that she was going to wed, so he assumed she had and refrained from making inquiries about her to anyone. And now all of it has turned out properly. And I played a role in causing it to happen. Maybe, just as Mrs. Sowerby claims, all things are predetermined and it was destined to occur regardless. Even if that is true, though, it feels pleasant to consider that one served as an agent employed by destiny. Yes indeed, it’s very romantic.”
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0005 }

“I don’t see how it’s so terribly romantic in any way,” Thirza remarked quite sharply. It was Thirza’s opinion that Nell was overly excited regarding the matter and possessed more than enough tasks preparing for college, rather than “traipsing” over to Echo Cottage two out of every three days to assist Miss Rosalind. “To begin with, a pair of young fools argue and act sullen; next, Steve Stanhope departs for the States and following a period of time marries over there, living completely happily according to every report. Subsequently his spouse passes away, and following an appropriate gap of time, he decides to return home to discover whether his initial crush will accept him. In the meantime, she has remained unmarried, likely due to no one sufficiently pleasant coming around to desire her, and the two meet and concur to wed in the end. So, what part of all that contains romance?”
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0006 }

“Oh, if you state it like that, there is no reason,” Nell sputtered, sounding almost as though she had been splashed with icy water. “I imagine it appears that way in prose. However, viewing it by way of poetry makes it quite different . . . and I believe it is far better . . .” Nell pulled herself together as her eyes sparkled and her face turned red . . . “viewing it by way of poetry.”
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0007 }

Thirza looked toward the glowing young visage and held back additional sharp remarks. It may be that she somewhat understood it was preferable, in the end, to possess, as Nell did, “the vision and the faculty divine” . . . that present which cannot be granted or stripped away by the world, of viewing existence by way of a transfiguring . . . or unmasking? . . . lens, through which all appeared dressed in heavenly radiance, carrying a brilliance and a novelty unseen by individuals who, such as herself and Belinda the Fourth, saw reality solely through prose.
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0008 }

“When is the wedding scheduled to take place?” she inquired following a brief silence.
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0009 }

“They will wed on the final Wednesday of August beneath the garden's honeysuckle trellis . . . precisely where Mr. Stanhope asked her to marry him a quarter of a century earlier. Thirza, even written down, that possesses romance. The only people present will be Mrs. Stanhope, Cedric, Hugh, Isolde, myself, and the cousins of Miss Rosalind. Following that, they are departing on the train at six o’clock for a journey to the Pacific coast. Upon returning in the autumn, Cedric along with Belinda the Fourth will move to Boston to reside alongside them. However, Echo Cottage will remain exactly as it stands. . . except naturally they will dispose of the cow and hens, shutter the windows . . . and each summer they intend to return and inhabit it. This makes me so happy. During the upcoming winter at Wexcombe, it would have pained me terribly to imagine that beloved stone home stripped bare and abandoned, filled with vacant rooms . . . or even more terrible, inhabited by strangers. Instead, I am able to envision it as I have always known it, patiently and joyfully awaiting the return of life and laughter with the coming summer.”
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0010 }

Greater romance existed in the world than the portion that had been granted to the middle-aged lovers residing in the stone house. Nell unexpectedly came across it one evening as she crossed over to Pear Hill through the wood cut and emerged into the Pembroke garden. Isolde Pembroke and Gideon Duckett were positioned beside one another beneath the large willow. Isolde was resting against the gray trunk, her eyelashes lowered over extremely crimson cheeks. A single hand was gripped by Gideon, who stood with his face turned down toward her, stammering a message in quiet, serious tones. No other individuals existed in the world besides the two of them during that enchanting moment; thus, neither one observed Nell, who, following a single stunned look of understanding, turned around and ran silently back through the spruce wood, refusing to halt until she reached her own gable room, where she sat out of breath by her window and attempted to gather her fragmented thoughts.
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0011 }

“Gideon and Isolde share a mutual love,” she breathed heavily. “Oh, it appears extremely . . . extremely . . . extremely mature.”
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0012 }

Lately, Nell had entertained certain doubts that Isolde was being unfaithful to the somber Byronic protagonist of her former reveries. However, because “things seen are mightier than things heard,” or surmised, the actual manifestation of this truth struck her with a force nearly resembling absolute astonishment. Following this, a strange, faint sense of isolation took hold . . . as though Isolde had somehow advanced into a fresh realm, closing a portal in her wake, and abandoning Nell on the exterior.
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0013 }

“Events are transforming with such speed that I am nearly terrified,” was the slightly sorrowful reflection of Nell. “Moreover, I fear that our relationship, Isolde's and mine, will inevitably be altered by this. My certainty is complete that I will be unable to share every one of my confidences with her following these events . . . she could reveal them to Gideon. Furthermore, what attraction does Gideon hold for her? Although he is quite pleasant and cheerful . . . his identity remains merely Gideon Duckett.”
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0014 }

The query of what one person perceives in another remains an enduringly perplexing mystery. Nevertheless, it is truly advantageous that human perspectives differ, because if all minds were in agreement, then, to quote the old Indian, “Everybody would want my squaw.” Regardless of how blinded Nell's vision was, Isolde undoubtedly discerned a special quality in Gideon Duckett. Arriving at Grey Shutters on the following night as a contemplative and timid maiden, Isolde shared the entire narrative with Nell within the shadowed privacy of the east gable. Tears were shed, kisses exchanged, and laughter shared by the two young women.
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0015 }

“I’m so happy,” Isolde said, “yet the idea of my engagement feels completely absurd.”
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0016 }

“How does it truly feel to be engaged?” Nell inquired with curiosity.
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0017 }

“Well, that relies entirely upon the person you’re engaged to,” Isolde replied, adopting that infuriating demeanor of higher intelligence ever exhibited by engaged individuals toward those who are single. “Being engaged to Gideon is absolutely wonderful . . . however, being engaged to anybody else would be downright terrible, in my opinion.”
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0018 }

“Seeing as Gideon is the only one, the rest of us cannot take much solace in that,” Nell chuckled.
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0019 }

“Oh, Nell, you fail to comprehend,” Isolde stated with annoyance. “I was not implying that . . . expressing it is quite difficult. Forget it, you will comprehend eventually, once it happens to you.”
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0020 }

“God bless you, most beloved Isolde, I comprehend at present. What purpose does a capacity for fantasy serve if it fails to permit one to glimpse existence using the sight of others?”
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0021 }

“You have to serve as my bridesmaid, Nell, you know. Make me a promise regarding that . . . no matter where you happen to be at the time of my marriage.”
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0022 }

“If required, I will travel from the furthest reaches of the globe,” Nell declared in a earnest manner.
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0023 }

“Naturally, it will not happen for a very long time,” Isolde stated, her cheeks turning red. “At minimum, three years . . . because my age is just eighteen and my mother declares that a daughter of hers will not wed until reaching twenty-one. Furthermore, Gideon’s father intends to purchase the Abraham Fletcher farm on his behalf, and he asserts that two thirds of the cost must be settled before he transfers the title to him. However, three years is hardly excessive for preparing a home, since I possess no handmade decorations whatsoever so far. Even so, I will start making crocheted doilies tomorrow. Myra Pettigrew possessed thirty-seven doilies upon her marriage, and I am set on having an equal number to hers.”
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0024 }

“I imagine that managing a home with a mere thirty-six doilies would be completely out of the question,” agreed Nell, her expression grave even as her eyes gleamed with mischief.
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0025 }

Isolde looked hurt.
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0026 }

“I expected you wouldn't mock me, Nell,” she remarked with disappointment.
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0027 }

“Dearest, I wasn’t making fun of you,” Nell exclaimed with regret. “I was merely teasing you a little. I believe you’ll be the sweetest tiny housekeeper anywhere. And I find it absolutely wonderful that you are already making plans for your home o’dreams.”
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0028 }

As soon as Nell had spoken the words, “home o’dreams,” her imagination was caught, and she at once started building one for herself. Naturally, it was inhabited by a perfect master who was dark, proud, and gloomy; yet strangely, Hugh Carrow continued to linger around as well, aiding her with hanging pictures, planning gardens, and completing various other chores that a proud and gloomy hero clearly felt were below him. Nell attempted to drive Hugh’s likeness away from her castle in Spain, but somehow he remained present, so Nell, feeling rushed, abandoned the effort and continued her imaginary construction so successfully that her “home o’dreams” stood erected and decorated before Isolde uttered another word.
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0029 }

“Nell, it must seem amusing to you, I imagine, that Gideon appeals to me so much when he is so unlike the sort of husband I always claimed I’d choose . . . the lean, towering type? Yet somehow, I’d prefer Gideon not to be lean and towering . . . since, you see, that would make him someone other than Gideon. To be sure,” Isolde continued with a somewhat mournful tone, “our pair will be terribly plump. Still, that beats a combination where one partner is squat and heavy while the other is towering and thin, similar to Varley Mott and his spouse. Mrs. Sowerby claims that seeing the two of them side by side perpetually reminds her of the long and short of it.”
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0030 }

"Well," Nell remarked inwardly during that evening, while combing her hair in front of her gilt framed glass, "Isolde's great joy and contentment make me glad. However, should my own moment arrive . . . assuming it ever will . . . I truly wish it will involve a bit more excitement. Then again, Isolde used to feel the same way. On numerous occasions, I have listened to her declare that she would refuse to become betrothed in any dull, ordinary manner . . . her suitor would need to perform a magnificent deed to gain her hand. Yet her mindset shifted. It is possible that my own views will shift as well. Still, I refuse to . . . and my resolve is firm that I will not. Oh, experiencing these betrothals among your close companions is, I believe, terribly disquieting."
{: #nw-v02-c29-p0031 }
